old: The standard rootstock for sweet oranges in California and the most common commercial choice. Resistant to Phytophthora root rot and tolerant of citrus tristeza virus. Produces vigorous, upright trees with good early bearing and excellent internal fruit quality. Not adapted to calcareous, highly alkaline, or saline soils. new: Carrizo is a citrange, a cross of Washington navel orange and trifoliate orange. UF/IFAS rates it a large, vigorous tree under Florida grove conditions. It tolerates tristeza virus, and UF/IFAS rates its Phytophthora tolerance intermediate. It does poorly in saline, high-pH and heavy clay soils, and it is susceptible to citrus nematode. old: A naturally dwarfing mutation of Poncirus trifoliata that produces very compact trees well suited to containers and small home gardens. Offers the best cold hardiness of any widely available citrus rootstock. Excellent resistance to Phytophthora, citrus nematode, and tristeza virus. Sensitive to high-pH and saline soils. Fruit quality is good and trees are precocious, though total yield per tree is lower due to small canopy size.
new: Flying Dragon is a trifoliate rootstock with a dwarfing effect of about 75 percent. UC Master Gardeners call it the only true dwarfing citrus rootstock, with trees 4 to 8 feet tall. UC Cooperative Extension calls it well suited to home and container citrus, but not to production orchards. UF/IFAS rates it tolerant of tristeza and Phytophthora, resistant to citrus nematode, and good in freezes. It does poorly in saline and high-pH soils. Its juice quality rates high, but small trees bear less fruit per tree.

old: A naturally dwarfing mutation of Poncirus trifoliata that produces very compact trees well suited to containers and small home gardens. Offers the best cold hardiness of any widely available citrus rootstock. Excellent resistance to Phytophthora, citrus nematode, and tristeza virus. Sensitive to high-pH and saline soils. Fruit quality is good and trees are precocious, though total yield per tree is lower due to small canopy size.
new: Flying Dragon is a trifoliate rootstock with a dwarfing effect of about 75 percent. UC Master Gardeners call it the only true dwarfing citrus rootstock, with trees 4 to 8 feet tall. UC Cooperative Extension calls it well suited to home and container citrus, but not to production orchards. UF/IFAS rates it tolerant of tristeza and Phytophthora, resistant to citrus nematode, and good in freezes. It does poorly in saline and high-pH soils. Its juice quality rates high, but small trees bear less fruit per tree.

old: Flying Dragon is a special dwarfing rootstock that keeps the tree small, which makes it perfect for pots and small yards. It also has the best cold hardiness of the common citrus rootstocks and strongly resists root rot. The tradeoff is simply a smaller tree with a smaller crop, which is usually exactly what a container or small-space grower wants.
new: Flying Dragon is a dwarfing rootstock that keeps a citrus tree small, usually 4 to 8 feet tall. That makes it a good fit for a pot or a small yard. It holds up well against tristeza virus, root rot and cold. Its fruit is good, but a smaller tree means a smaller crop. It does poorly in salty or alkaline soil.

old: Grapefruit grows vigorously and yields well on Swingle citrumelo, which resists Phytophthora and citrus nematode and tolerates the tristeza virus that killed off the once-standard sour orange rootstock for grapefruit. Sour orange still produces excellent grapefruit where tristeza is not a threat. For containers or small spaces, Flying Dragon trifoliate makes a dwarf tree. Ask the nursery which rootstock the tree is on and match it to your soil, since Swingle and trifoliate types dislike high-pH, calcareous, or saline soils common in the desert.
new: Swingle citrumelo is particularly well adapted to grapefruit. It resists Phytophthora foot rot and citrus nematode, and it tolerates tristeza, a virus that can kill citrus trees quickly. Rootstocks are usually not a choice at retail garden centers, so ask which one your tree is on. For a pot or a small yard, Flying Dragon makes a dwarf tree. Swingle does poorly in calcareous soil, and Flying Dragon does poorly in high-pH soil.

old.summary: Grapefruit-drug interaction (furanocoumarin/CYP3A4 inhibition affecting statins, some blood-pressure, anti-anxiety, and transplant drugs) is a well-documented consumer-safety fact but was NOT asserted in consumer prose because no clean Tier-1 university-extension/.edu page could be read via WebFetch this session (searches surfaced FDA + medical-journal sources only; the FDA consumer page 404'd on fetch). Flagged per brief rather than asserted; certify session should source it from a T1/authoritative page and add an honest note.

Two key source pages could not be cleanly WebFetched: the Texas A&M AgriLife grapefruit page (aggie-hort.tamu.edu/citrus/grapefruit.htm) hit an http/https + host redirect loop, and the University of Arizona pages (extension.arizona.edu low-desert-citrus 403; AZ1925 grapefruit-pummelo is a 5.3MB scanned PDF not machine-readable). Their grapefruit claims (Texas variety history Ruby Red/Rio Red/Star Ruby/Duncan; desert 9-13 month ripening and long-hang sweetening) were corroborated via multiple WebSearch summaries but not read from a single clean page; confirm at certify.

Per-cell cold bands (min_winter_temp_f) and the heat_summer_basis verdicts were modeled from grapefruit's documented cold-hardiness rank (below sweet orange, wood damage mid-20s°F, fruit 26-28°F per LSU/UGA) and its documented high-heat need, applied to each region's climate, not from a grapefruit-specific per-region freeze/heat table. Edges are best-effort; tighten at variety-delta pass.

ca_north_coast modeled as survives_no_fruit/insufficient with an EMPTY calendar (a sharper call than navel orange's marginal), on the judgment that grapefruit's much higher heat requirement means the coolest CA coast produces no dependable edible crop. ca_south_coast kept marginal/marginal with a long-hang calendar. Confirm the coastal split against a CA-coast grapefruit source at review.

hawaii_tropical is lowest-confidence: modeled marginal/marginal (warm humid tropical lowland lacks the heat accumulation and day-night swing that sweetens grapefruit; pummelo does better), cited to UH CTAHR generally rather than a grapefruit-specific Hawaii calendar. Regional harvest windows across all 10 regions are modeled from the nearest readable citrus source plus grapefruit's long-hang biology, not a grapefruit-specific regional planting chart.

Pests/diseases and rootstock sourcing lean on citrus-general Tier-1 pages (uc_ipm citrus, uf_ifas_hs132/edis), re-tuned for grapefruit emphasis (rust mite russeting, melanose, greasy-spot and canker susceptibility, faster HLB decline; Swingle citrumelo / sour orange rootstock notes), rather than grapefruit-only trials. Companions are traditional/low-confidence citrus guild items plus the grounded grass-competition avoid. Rootstock recommendation (Swingle citrumelo) modeled from citrus-general guidance.

mature_height_ft / mature_spread_ft left null at PLA-465 promote 1. The retired UF/IFAS HS982 (read from an LSU-hosted copy) gives 15 to 20 ft for grapefruit on standard rootstocks; the live UF/IFAS HS1260 rates Swingle citrumelo, the crop's recommended rootstock, 'I, 8 to 14 ft tall' (in-row spacing 8-12 ft), while LSU pub 1234 calls Swingle 'very vigorous'; the crop's own rootstock row carries 12-20. No page states a grapefruit spread.
old.resolution_note: Trevor's ruling 2026-09-17: UNUSABLE SOURCE, null, no derivation attempted. Two sources in conflict anchor neither figure.
